sectionTitle: Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)
topic: Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity.
The voltage produced by a cell is dependent upon a number of factors including the type of electrode and electrolyte.
A simple cell can be made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte.
Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage.
In non-rechargeable cells and batteries the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.
Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied.
Students should be able to interpret data for relative reactivity of different metals and evaluate the use of cells.
Students do not need to know details of cells and batteries other than those specified.
Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air. The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference.
The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water.
Hydrogen fuel cells offer a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries.
evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells in comparison with rechargeable cells and batteries
(HT only) write the half equations for the electrode reactions in the hydrogen fuel cell.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know details of cells and batteries other than those specified.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nothing in this topic goes beyond the cells and batteries the specification itself names. Cell chemistry is treated only at the level of 'two different metals in contact with an electrolyte'; the only named battery type is the alkaline battery, and it appears only to make the specification's own point that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable. No item asks for the internal chemistry, construction, named electrode materials or reaction equations of any commercial cell (zinc-carbon, lithium-ion, lead-acid, nickel-cadmium), for standard electrode potentials, or for the salt bridge and electrochemical series treatment used at A-level. Where reactivity data are used (q09) the voltages are given in the question to be interpreted, not recalled. The only equations required are the overall hydrogen fuel cell reaction and, for Higher Tier, the two electrode half equations.

concepts.definition: A chemical cell contains chemicals which react together to produce electricity. The electricity is not stored inside the cell beforehand: it is produced by the reaction, and only while the reaction can continue and the circuit is complete.

One of the two conducting solids, usually metals, that dip into the electrolyte and are connected into the external circuit. The type of electrode used is one of the factors that determines the voltage a cell produces.
The conducting liquid or paste in which the electrodes are placed. It contains ions that can move, and the type of electrolyte used is one of the factors that determines the voltage a cell produces.

The potential difference produced across the two electrodes of a cell. It depends upon a number of factors, including the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte, not upon how large the cell is.

A cell made by connecting two different metals that are in contact with an electrolyte. The two metals must be different: two identical electrodes react with the electrolyte in the same way and produce no voltage.
Two or more cells connected together in series. Connecting cells in series provides a greater voltage than a single cell, because the voltages of the individual cells add together.
Cells joined end to end so that the same current passes through each one in turn. Joined this way their voltages add, which is why a battery of four 1.5 V cells provides 6.0 V.

A cell in which the chemical reactions cannot be reversed. The reactions stop, and the cell stops producing a voltage, when one of the reactants has been used up. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.
The named example of a non-rechargeable battery in this specification. It cannot be recharged: once one of its reactants has been used up the reactions stop and the battery is replaced.

A cell that can be recharged because the chemical reactions inside it are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. No new chemicals are added and no waste is removed; the products are turned back into reactants.

In a cell made from two different metals in an electrolyte, the greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage produced. This allows voltages for untested pairs to be predicted from reactivity data.

A cell that is supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air. The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the cell to produce a potential difference, and the cell keeps working for as long as the fuel and oxygen are supplied.

Oxidation carried out at an electrode so that the electrons lost by the fuel travel round the external circuit. This is what allows a fuel cell to produce a potential difference directly, rather than releasing the energy as heat by burning.
The overall reaction is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Water is the only product of the reaction in the cell.

An equation showing what happens at one electrode, including the electrons. In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte the negative electrode reaction is H2 → 2H+ + 2e− and the positive electrode reaction is O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O. Both atoms and charges must balance.

Weighing advantages against disadvantages using evidence: for cells, cost, lifetime, whether they can be recharged and how they are disposed of; for hydrogen fuel cells, the fact that only water is produced set against the difficulty and cost of storing and distributing hydrogen.

misconceptions.question: Where is the electricity in a cell before it is connected?
misconceptions.correct: Nowhere. Electricity is produced by the reaction between the chemicals once the circuit is complete.
misconceptions.misconception: A cell is a container filled with electricity, and using the cell drains out the electricity that was put in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language treats batteries as full or empty, and circuit diagrams show charge flowing out of the cell, which invites the picture of a tank being emptied.
misconceptions.correction: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity. Nothing flows until the circuit is complete; the reaction then produces the electricity.

misconceptions.question: Two cells use the same metals but one is twice the size. Do they give different voltages?
misconceptions.correct: No. The voltage depends on the type of electrode and electrolyte, not on how much of each there is.
misconceptions.misconception: A bigger cell, or one with more electrolyte, must produce a bigger voltage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students conflate voltage with how long a cell lasts. A larger cell does hold more reactant and so lasts longer, which is read as being more powerful.
misconceptions.correction: The voltage produced by a cell is dependent upon factors including the type of electrode and electrolyte. Size affects lifetime and current, not the voltage.

misconceptions.question: Does using thicker connecting wire change the voltage of a cell?
misconceptions.correct: No. The voltage comes from the reaction between the chemicals, not from the circuit outside the cell.
misconceptions.misconception: The voltage is a property of the circuit and the wires, so changing the connections changes the voltage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Voltage is first met as something measured across components in a circuit, so it is attached to the circuit rather than to the chemistry that generates it.
misconceptions.correction: The voltage is set by the type of electrode and electrolyte. The external wire only provides a path for the current.

misconceptions.question: Would zinc and copper in pure water make a working cell?
misconceptions.correct: No. Pure water has almost no ions to carry charge, so it does not act as an electrolyte.
misconceptions.misconception: Any liquid will do as the electrolyte, because the current just needs something to travel through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show the metals in a beaker of clear liquid, and students see the liquid as a gap-filler rather than as a chemical taking part.
misconceptions.correction: A simple cell needs two different metals in contact with an electrolyte, and the type of electrolyte affects the voltage produced.

misconceptions.question: Will two copper strips in an electrolyte produce a voltage?
misconceptions.correct: No. A simple cell needs two different metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Any two electrodes in an electrolyte make a cell, so two pieces of the same metal will work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electrolysis is met first, where two identical carbon or platinum electrodes are normal, so students carry that arrangement over to cells.
misconceptions.correction: A simple cell can be made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Identical electrodes react with the electrolyte in the same way, so there is no voltage.

misconceptions.question: Is a large copper strip with a small copper strip a simple cell?
misconceptions.correct: No. The electrodes must be different metals, not the same metal in different sizes.
misconceptions.misconception: 'Two different electrodes' means two electrodes that differ in some way, such as their size or shape.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'different' is read loosely, and students know that changing the size of an electrode does change the current, so they assume it changes the voltage too.
misconceptions.correction: The specification requires two different metals. Changing the area of an electrode alters the current a cell can supply, not the voltage it produces.

misconceptions.question: Four 1.5 V cells are joined in series. What is the battery voltage?
misconceptions.correct: 6.0 V. The voltages of the cells in series add together.
misconceptions.misconception: The cells share out a single voltage, so the battery gives 1.5 V, or even less than that.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and the supply voltage is shared between the components, and this sharing rule is applied to the cells themselves.
misconceptions.correction: Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage. Four 1.5 V cells give 6.0 V.

misconceptions.question: Why does connecting cells in series give a greater voltage?
misconceptions.correct: Because the voltage of each cell adds to the voltage of the next.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the current supplied by each cell adds up, and more current means more voltage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Current and voltage are not clearly separated, so any statement about 'more' from more cells is expressed in terms of current.
misconceptions.correction: Cells in series provide a greater voltage. The current through cells in series is the same through each one; it is the voltages that add.

misconceptions.question: Why does a non-rechargeable cell go flat?
misconceptions.correct: Because one of the reactants inside it has been used up, so the reactions stop.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the cell has run out of electricity, or run out of the electrons it was holding.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The tank model of a battery survives into this topic: the cell is imagined as a store of charge that empties with use.
misconceptions.correction: In non-rechargeable cells and batteries the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up.

misconceptions.question: Must every reactant be used up before a cell stops working?
misconceptions.correct: No. The reactions stop as soon as one of the reactants has been used up.
misconceptions.misconception: A cell keeps going until everything inside it, both electrodes and the electrolyte, has been used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the cell running down evenly, rather than one reactant running out first while the rest is left unreacted.
misconceptions.correction: The chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up; the other reactants are simply left over.

misconceptions.question: Can an alkaline battery be recharged?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkaline batteries are rechargeable, because they last longer and sound more advanced than ordinary ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Advertising stresses how long alkaline cells last, and rechargeable AA cells look identical to alkaline AA cells on the shelf.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable: their reactions cannot be reversed, so they are replaced when flat.

misconceptions.question: What happens inside a rechargeable cell while it is being recharged?
misconceptions.correct: The chemical reactions that ran during use are reversed by the external current.
misconceptions.misconception: Recharging refills the cell: new reactants are pushed in, or the used-up chemical is topped up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Recharge' shares its everyday meaning with refilling a tank, and students have no picture of a reaction being driven backwards.
misconceptions.correction: Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied.

misconceptions.question: How does the voltage of a cell depend on the two metals used?
misconceptions.correct: The bigger the difference in reactivity between the metals, the bigger the voltage.
misconceptions.misconception: The voltage depends only on how reactive one of the metals is, or a smaller reactivity gap gives a bigger voltage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students latch onto a single metal in the pair, usually the more reactive one, instead of comparing the two, and reverse the direction of the trend.
misconceptions.correction: The voltage rises as the difference in reactivity of the two metals rises. A metal only just above copper in the reactivity series gives a small voltage with copper.

misconceptions.question: Can the voltages of two cells in a table be added to predict a third?
misconceptions.correct: No. Adding them is wrong: predict the voltage from where the metals lie in the reactivity series.
misconceptions.misconception: Any two numbers in the table can be added, or combined in any order, to give the voltage of a new pair.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Data questions invite arithmetic, so students combine the numbers in front of them rather than reasoning from the reactivity order.
misconceptions.correction: Adding the values is always wrong. If both cells share the same second electrode, the difference between two values gives the cell made from the other two metals (2.7 V - 1.1 V = 1.6 V for magnesium and zinc). For a metal that is not in the table, use its position in the reactivity series instead.

misconceptions.question: Does a hydrogen fuel cell need recharging?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is supplied with hydrogen and oxygen from outside and works for as long as they are supplied.
misconceptions.misconception: A fuel cell is just a large battery: its energy is stored inside it and it has to be recharged when it runs down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fuel cells are met immediately after rechargeable cells, and both are drawn as a box in a circuit, so the external fuel supply is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air. Nothing is stored in the cell and no recharging is involved.

misconceptions.question: How does a fuel cell turn hydrogen into a potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrogen is oxidised electrochemically at an electrode, so the electrons it loses pass round the circuit.
misconceptions.misconception: The hydrogen is burned inside the cell and the heat produced drives a small generator.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hydrogen is known as a fuel that burns, and the only familiar way of getting electricity from a fuel is to burn it in a power station.
misconceptions.correction: The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference; there is no burning and no generator.

misconceptions.question: Is hydrogen oxidised or reduced in a hydrogen fuel cell?
misconceptions.correct: Oxidised. Hydrogen gains oxygen inside the cell to form water.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen is reduced, because it combines with oxygen and gains something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxidation is remembered as 'gaining oxygen', but the gain is hidden inside the cell, and the word 'reduced' is attached to the fuel because the fuel is used up.
misconceptions.correction: The fuel is oxidised in a fuel cell and it is the oxygen that is reduced. (HT only: the half equation for the fuel is H2 → 2H+ + 2e−.)

misconceptions.question: Is a hydrogen fuel cell the same as the electrolysis of water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Electrolysis uses a current to split water; a fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen and supplies a current.
misconceptions.misconception: The fuel cell splits water inside itself, or needs a current supplied to it to work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two are taught close together and use the same apparatus in demonstrations, so the direction of the process is confused.
misconceptions.correction: A fuel cell is supplied with fuel from outside and produces a potential difference. Electrolysis is the reverse process and consumes electricity.

misconceptions.question: What is produced in a hydrogen fuel cell?
misconceptions.correct: Water only.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen peroxide is produced, or carbon dioxide like any other fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: H2O2 looks like a reasonable product from H2 and O2, and 'fuel' is associated with the carbon dioxide given off by burning petrol.
misconceptions.correction: The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

misconceptions.question: What must be balanced in a half equation?
misconceptions.correct: Both the atoms and the charges on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: A half equation only needs the atoms to match, so the number of electrons can be chosen freely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electrons are treated as an optional extra written on the end, rather than as charged particles that have to be counted.
misconceptions.correction: In H2 → 2H+ + 2e− the two hydrogen atoms balance and the charge is zero on both sides. In O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O the charges also cancel.

misconceptions.question: Which electrode does H2 → 2H+ + 2e− describe?
misconceptions.correct: The negative electrode, where hydrogen is oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: The two electrode equations can be swapped, or the acidic and alkaline versions mixed together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two half equations are learned as a pair without being tied to what is happening chemically at each electrode, so their labels and forms get exchanged.
misconceptions.correction: At the negative electrode hydrogen loses electrons: H2 → 2H+ + 2e−. At the positive electrode oxygen gains them: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O.

misconceptions.question: Does a hydrogen fuel cell car give out carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Not from the cell itself. The only product is water.
misconceptions.misconception: A fuel cell car gives out carbon dioxide from its exhaust, because all fuels release carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every fuel students have met, from methane to petrol, contains carbon, so carbon dioxide is treated as the automatic product of any fuel.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen contains no carbon, so the cell produces only water. Carbon dioxide may be released elsewhere, when the hydrogen is manufactured.

misconceptions.question: Once a fuel cell has started, does it need anything supplied to it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It needs a continuous supply of fuel and of oxygen or air.
misconceptions.misconception: Once the reaction has started it keeps itself going and needs nothing further.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The cell is imagined as being switched on like a battery, so the continuous external supply that defines a fuel cell is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air. Stop either supply and the cell stops producing a potential difference.

misconceptions.question: How is a symbol equation such as 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O balanced?
misconceptions.correct: Only by putting numbers in front of formulae, then checking both sides again.
misconceptions.misconception: An equation can be balanced by adding a spare atom on the end, changing a formula, or fixing one side and stopping there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is treated as making the totals agree by any available means, and students who alter the right-hand side often do not go back and re-check the left.
misconceptions.correction: Put numbers in front of the formulae, then count every element on both sides: H2 + O2 → 2H2O leaves the hydrogen unbalanced. Writing H2O + O does make the atoms tally, but it invents a lone oxygen atom that is not a product, so it is still wrong.

mcqs.stem: A chemical cell is connected to a lamp and the lamp lights. Where does the electricity come from?

options.text: From chemicals inside the cell that react together
options.rationale: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity; the reaction runs only once the circuit is complete.

options.text: From electricity stored in the cell already
options.rationale: The everyday picture of a battery as a tank of electricity waiting to be poured out.

options.text: From a store of electrons in the metal casing
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a cell holds a fixed stock of electrons that gradually runs out.

options.text: From the air reacting with the outer case
options.rationale: Confuses an ordinary chemical cell with a fuel cell, which is fed oxygen or air from outside.

mcqs.stem: Two cells are identical except that one uses zinc and copper electrodes and the other uses magnesium and copper. The cells give different voltages. Why?

options.text: The voltage depends on how much electrolyte there is
options.rationale: Students often assume a bigger cell means a bigger voltage, confusing voltage with how long the cell lasts.

options.text: The voltage depends on the type of electrode used
options.rationale: The voltage produced by a cell depends on a number of factors, including the type of electrode.

options.text: The voltage depends on the area of the electrode
options.rationale: Surface area affects the current a cell can deliver, not the voltage it produces.

options.text: The voltage depends on the wire joining them up
options.rationale: The connecting wire completes the circuit but takes no part in the reaction that produces the voltage.

mcqs.stem: A simple cell uses zinc and copper electrodes in copper sulfate solution. The copper sulfate solution is replaced by a different electrolyte, with everything else unchanged. What happens to the voltage?

options.text: It stays the same, because only the metals matter here
options.rationale: Students remember that different metals give different voltages and conclude the electrolyte is irrelevant.

options.text: It stays the same for any liquid, even for pure water
options.rationale: Assumes any liquid conducts, so the choice of electrolyte cannot matter.

options.text: It may change, as the voltage depends on electrolyte
options.rationale: The voltage produced by a cell depends on the type of electrolyte as well as the type of electrode.

options.text: It changes only if the new electrolyte is an acid
options.rationale: Over-generalises from lessons where acids are used as electrolytes; other electrolytes work too.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of electrodes, dipped into an electrolyte, would produce a voltage?

options.text: Two identical strips of copper metal
options.rationale: Two electrodes of the same metal react with the electrolyte in the same way, so no voltage is produced.

options.text: Two copper strips of different size
options.rationale: Treats 'different electrodes' as meaning different sizes rather than different metals.

options.text: Two carbon rods taken from cells
options.rationale: Carbon rods are used in electrolysis, but two identical electrodes cannot give a voltage.

options.text: A zinc strip and a copper strip
options.rationale: A simple cell is made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: A battery is made by connecting four 1.5 V cells together in series. What voltage does the battery provide, and why?

options.text: 1.5 V, because the cells share one voltage
options.rationale: Confuses the series rule for voltage with the way current is the same all round a series circuit.

options.text: 6.0 V, because the voltages of the cells add up
options.rationale: Batteries consist of two or more cells connected in series to provide a greater voltage.

options.text: 6.0 V, because the current from each cell adds
options.rationale: Right value, wrong reasoning: in series it is the voltages that add, not the currents.

options.text: 0.375 V, as the voltage is split between them
options.rationale: Applies the idea of sharing voltage between components to the cells themselves.

mcqs.stem: A non-rechargeable cell stops producing a voltage after some time in use. Why does it stop?

options.text: All the electrons inside the cell have been used up
options.rationale: Pictures the cell as a container of electrons that empties, rather than as a chemical reaction.

options.text: The electrolyte has leaked out of its case
options.rationale: A real but unusual fault, not the reason every non-rechargeable cell goes flat.

options.text: One of the reactants has been completely used up
options.rationale: In non-rechargeable cells the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up.

options.text: Both of the electrodes have been fully used up
options.rationale: Only one reactant needs to run out for the reaction, and so the voltage, to stop.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about alkaline batteries is correct?

options.text: They can be recharged from the mains many times over
options.rationale: Alkaline cells last longer than zinc-carbon cells, which students misread as being rechargeable.

options.text: They are rechargeable once the alkali is replaced
options.rationale: Assumes recharging means topping up a chemical rather than reversing the reactions.

options.text: They give a voltage only while being recharged
options.rationale: Confuses the cell being recharged with the cell being used.

options.text: They are non-rechargeable, so they are replaced
options.rationale: The specification states that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.

mcqs.stem: A rechargeable cell is connected to an external electrical supply. What happens inside the cell?

options.text: The chemical reactions are reversed
options.rationale: Rechargeable cells can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external current is supplied.

options.text: Fresh reactants are pushed into the cell
options.rationale: Imagines recharging as refilling the cell with new chemicals from outside.

options.text: Extra electrons are stored inside it
options.rationale: Treats charge as something stockpiled in the cell rather than a reaction being driven backwards.

options.text: The used-up reactants are all removed
options.rationale: Nothing leaves a sealed rechargeable cell; the products are turned back into reactants.

mcqs.stem: Cells are made from a copper electrode and one other metal in the same electrolyte. The voltages are: magnesium 2.7 V, zinc 1.1 V, iron 0.8 V. Tin is less reactive than iron but more reactive than copper. What voltage would a tin and copper cell most likely give?

options.text: About 1.9 V, from the zinc and iron values added
options.rationale: Combines two numbers from the table instead of reasoning from the reactivity order.

options.text: About 3.4 V, since tin is the least reactive metal
options.rationale: Inverts the pattern: a smaller reactivity difference gives a smaller voltage, not a larger one.

options.text: About 0.5 V, because tin is close to copper in reactivity
options.rationale: The voltage rises with the difference in reactivity, so tin, just above copper, gives a small voltage.

options.text: About 2.7 V, the same as the magnesium cell gives
options.rationale: Assumes every cell containing copper gives the same voltage, ignoring the second metal.

mcqs.stem: Where does the hydrogen in a hydrogen fuel cell come from?

options.text: It is stored inside the cell when the cell is built
options.rationale: Treats a fuel cell like a battery, with its chemicals sealed inside from the start.

options.text: It is made inside the cell from air and water
options.rationale: Invents an internal source rather than an external supply of fuel.

options.text: It is released by the electrolyte as it runs
options.rationale: Confuses the fuel cell with electrolysis, where hydrogen is produced from the solution.

options.text: It is fed in from an external supply of the fuel
options.rationale: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air.

mcqs.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell, how does the fuel produce a potential difference?

options.text: It is oxidised electrochemically at an electrode
options.rationale: The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference.

options.text: It is burned, and the heat drives a generator
options.rationale: Describes a power station or engine; a fuel cell produces a potential difference directly.

options.text: It is reduced by oxygen at the negative electrode
options.rationale: Reverses the chemistry: hydrogen is oxidised, and it is oxygen that is reduced.

options.text: It is decomposed by a current supplied to the cell
options.rationale: Describes electrolysis, where a current is supplied, rather than a cell that supplies one.

mcqs.stem: Which equation represents the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?

options.text: H2 + O2 → H2O + O
options.rationale: The atoms do tally, but a lone oxygen atom is not a product: the only product is water.
The overall reaction is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water, balanced as 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.
Gives hydrogen peroxide instead of water; the only product of a hydrogen fuel cell is water.

options.text: H2 + O2 → 2H2O
options.rationale: Right products, but the hydrogen atoms are not balanced: two on the left, four on the right.

mcqs.stem: Why are hydrogen fuel cells described as a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries?

options.text: They can be refilled with electricity at any charge point
options.rationale: Fuel cells are refuelled with hydrogen; it is batteries that are refilled with electricity.

options.text: They store far more electricity inside them than a battery
options.rationale: A fuel cell stores no electricity at all; the energy comes from the fuel supplied to it.

options.text: They need no fuel or oxygen once they have been started
options.rationale: A fuel cell stops the moment the external supply of fuel or oxygen stops.

options.text: They keep working while hydrogen is supplied, with no recharging
options.rationale: A fuel cell runs on an external fuel supply, so it does not have to be taken out of use to recharge.

mcqs.stem: A car maker compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a rechargeable battery car. Which is a genuine disadvantage of the fuel cell car?

options.text: It gives out carbon dioxide as it is driven
options.rationale: A hydrogen fuel cell produces only water; carbon dioxide comes from burning fuels containing carbon.

options.text: Hydrogen is difficult to store safely
options.rationale: Hydrogen is a flammable gas that must be stored under pressure or at very low temperature, which is a real drawback.

options.text: It must be plugged in and recharged often
options.rationale: Recharging is the battery's limitation, not the fuel cell's.

options.text: It stops once its battery has gone flat
options.rationale: A fuel cell has no battery to go flat; it runs while fuel is supplied.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode?

options.rationale: The hydrogen atoms are not balanced: four on the left and two on the right.
Uses water as the reactant, as in the electrolysis of water, and leaves the oxygen unaccounted for.
Hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode, losing electrons: H2 → 2H+ + 2e−.
The alkaline form of the equation, and with the electrons missing the charges do not balance.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the positive electrode?

options.rationale: Oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode, gaining electrons: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O.
Gives hydrogen peroxide rather than water, and the oxygen atoms do not balance.
The oxygen atoms are not balanced: two on the left and one on the right.
Neither the atoms nor the charges balance.

mcqs.stem: A games controller is used every day and flattens its cells within a week. Which is the best reason for choosing rechargeable cells for it?

options.text: They can be reused many times, so fewer cells are bought
options.rationale: With heavy daily use the cost and waste of replacing cells each week outweigh the higher purchase price of a rechargeable cell.

options.text: Recharging pushes new chemicals in, so they never wear out
options.rationale: Recharging reverses the reactions inside a sealed cell; nothing is added, and rechargeable cells do wear out in the end.

options.text: They hold much more electricity inside them when new
options.rationale: No cell holds electricity; it is produced by the reaction. This is the tank picture of a battery again.

options.text: They cost less to buy than an alkaline cell does
options.rationale: Rechargeable cells cost more to buy. The saving comes from reusing one cell instead of buying many.
